In any sort of functional anarchism, individual liberties would not be protected - they'd be granted.

What I mean - the entire approach to the concept of liberty is going to have to change in order for anarchism to work. Any approach that involves "protecting" liberty is inevitably going to devolve into punishing transgressors, which will lead fairly directly to authoritarianism. Instead, people are going to have to come to understand that liberty is not something that they force other people to grant them, but something that they grant to other people. That's the direction from which the issue has to be approached in order to guarantee rights.

Consider this:

Tom and Bob live on a desert island. Tom believes that he - Tom - possesses a right to life. Bob doesn't think there's such a thing as a right to life. Does Tom then possess a meaningful right to life?

Tom and Bob live on a desert island. Bob believes that Tom possesses a right to life. Does Tom then possess a meaningful right to life?

It's not sufficient that one insist that one possesses rights oneself. That's not the way it does or even can work, since whether or not one really does possess any truly meaningful rights is entirely in the hands of others - if they don't believe that you possess those rights, then your belief is utterly meaningless. It doesn't matter how strong or reasonable your belief is - if others will not cede you those rights, you do not in fact possess them. However, if others believe that you do possess those rights, then for all intents and purposes, you in fact do. That's exactly what it hinges on - people focusing not on their own purported rights, but on the rights of others. That's the only thing that will actually make them meaningful, and particularly in a society defined by the absence of mechanisms of authority. So the only meaningful thing that you can do regarding rights is cede them to others. And when everyone around you becomes aware of that and does the same, then AND ONLY THEN will you actually have rights.

And yes - humanity in general is a long, long way away from being able to actually do that, which is exactly why I believe that humanity in general is a long, long way away from being able to maintain an actual anarchism.

Terrorism Act incompatible with human rights, court rules in David Miranda case

I'm American but think this case is still highly interesting for those outside the UK. The UK doesn't have a Bill of Rights, or even a written Constitution. Freedom of speech, of association, from undue search and seizure, etc. are at best laudable goals and not something the government can be held to task when they don't abide by what Americans have codified as innate human rights.

A journalist suspected of carrying documents from the Snowden leak was held by police at Heathrow Airport for nine hours under a law designed to permit detaining terrorists. No right to remain silent. No right to an attorney. The UK equivalents of the ACLU joined his legal defense. Upon appeal, the judges ruled holding a journalist under a anti-terrorism law required that the police actually believed him to be a terrorist, not a journalist reporting on a whistle blower. The court further issued a "certificate of incompatibility" (invalidated the law as our Supremes have done since Marbury v. Madison) as the terrorism law's arbitrary detention clause conflicted with European human rights law.

All in all, this looks to this American like a striking blow for freedom.
